title: Assessment of the phytoconstituents and optimal applicable concentration of aqueous extract of Azadirachta indica leaves for wound healing in male Wistar rats

original_source.central_claim: aqueous neem leaf extract wound-healing activity and the specific 1.5% w/v optimum in male Wistar rats

central_claims: The tested aqueous neem-leaf extract contains multiple phytochemical classes and promotes excision-wound healing in male Wistar rats.
Among six tested concentrations, 1.5% w/v is the optimum inferred from tissue hydroxyproline; this particular concentration claim is distinct from generic neem wound-healing activity.

source_manifest.title: Assessment of the phytoconstituents and optimal applicable concentration of aqueous extract of Azadirachta indica leaves for wound healing in male Wistar rats
source_manifest.finding: Seven groups of five rats received aqueous extract concentrations or water; 1.5% w/v had the highest tissue hydroxyproline and is claimed optimal.

source_manifest.title: Evaluation of the Wound Healing Potentials of Aqueous Topical Creams Containing Aqueous Extract of Azadirachta indica Leaves as Bioactive Ingredient
source_manifest.finding: Same five original authors plus another author test creams containing 1, 1.5, 2 and 3% w/w extract; the highest reported hydroxyproline is at 1.5%. Independent validation is not established.

source_manifest.title: An assessment of the wound healing potential of a herbal gel containing an Azadirachta indica leaf extract
source_manifest.finding: Independent team tests ethanolic extract gels in rabbits; 3% w/w performs best among 1, 2 and 3%. This is a different solvent, formulation, species and dose set, not a test of the target aqueous 1.5% optimum.

source_manifest.title: A review of selected herbs responsible for wound management
source_manifest.finding: Its neem table and reference list adopt the topical cream paper, not the assigned aqueous concentration study.

answers.rationale: Independent rabbit experiments support generic neem activity, but use ethanol extract and a different optimum. They do not verify the assigned aqueous-extract optimum and phytochemical profile.
The closest matching 1.5% cream report shares the original authors; the independent gel experiment uses ethanol and rabbits. No independent reproduction of the aqueous 1.5% result was established.
The cream experiment still uses groups of five rats, and chronology relative to the target is uncertain. No larger or stricter direct test of the original optimum was verified.

The independent 3% ethanolic-gel optimum is neither confirmation nor refutation of a 1.5% aqueous optimum. No assessment directly retaining or overturning the original concentration claim was located.
No read follow-up establishes that the optimum survives larger samples, blinded evaluation, extract standardization or clinical wound settings.
The closest cream development shares the original team. The independent gel work does not establish a derivation from the target study.
Two independent teams substantively building on the assigned aqueous concentration study were not verified; generic neem research predates it.
The cream paper uses closely related methods but overlapping authors; independent reuse of this particular concentration-selection procedure was not established.
The 2023 review discusses herbal wound management and cites the related cream paper; it does not credit the assigned paper with starting a direction.
The rabbit study compares its own gels with nitrofurazone, but does not use the assigned aqueous 1.5% treatment as a benchmark.
No independent application demonstrates benefit from selecting the concentration established in the target study.
Creams and rabbit gels extend neem formulations generally; successful transfer of this paper’s specific aqueous optimum was not independently established.

The same-team cream study is a plausible related development, but its February 2021 date and the target PDF’s conflicting publication metadata prevent establishing a later result enabled by the target.
No official clinical, veterinary or manufacturing workflow adopting this paper’s concentration was verified.
No matched independent comparison verifies the stated advantage of 1.5% aqueous extract over the other five aqueous concentrations.
No substantive use of this particular concentration study from 2024 onward was verified; generic citations or use of other neem preparations do not settle the question.
The 2023 review is under three years later and reviews the cream paper. No qualifying later positive assessment of the assigned contribution was verified.
The read 2021 experiments and 2023 review do not establish independent substantive follow-up of the assigned paper in two separate years.
The closest review summarizes the different cream experiment. It does not establish synthesis adoption of the assigned concentration study.
No comparison with later wound-healing treatments explicitly establishes continued usefulness of this paper’s concentration finding.

search_gaps: Publisher abstract and substantial original PDF sections covering rationale, methods, phytochemical results and conclusion were read. Repeated PDF timeouts and publisher 403 prevented reading all remaining results pages; scope is explicitly partial.
Original PDF publication line and archive metadata are inconsistent within 2021; no causal follow-up credit is inferred from uncertain same-year ordering.
A 2022 cream report under different authors had closely matching indexed design text, but its full PDF returned 404; independence and provenance could not be verified and it is not counted.
No verified human trial or independent standardized-dose replication was located; this is an evidence gap, not proof of failure.
Lifetime observation through 2026-09-16; the assigned pilot sample is not an unbiased estimate of all research outcomes.
research.summary: Independent validation or adoption of the specific aqueous 1.5% optimum remains unresolved. A closely related cream paper shares the original authors; independent rabbit work uses ethanolic extract and different doses. All 20 outcomes remain unknown.
